body: Bolivia has short, white licence plates with blue text, which can appear plain white due to blurring.
All of Bolivia’s Street View coverage was captured by a white Google car with no antenna (Generation 3).
Many Bolivian buildings use large red bricks and often look unfinished, a style also found in Peru.
Bolivian middle road lines can be yellow, white, or a mix. Outer road lines are always white.
Concrete slab roads are fairly common in Bolivia, alongside standard asphalt roads.
Many Bolivian roads are made of cobblestone, often with a neat pattern of lined stones.
Bolivia uses bulky, white square signposts, unlike Peru's zebra-striped signposts.
Guardrails sometimes have yellow and black markings, with yellow on the outside.
Bolivia has round concrete and wooden utility poles, with variable tops; Argentina-style poles appear rarely.
Wooden poles in eastern Bolivia are often extremely curvy, made from local tree trunks.
Bolivian kilometre markers are black and white, with 'Km' on top and distance on the bottom, but no road numbers.
Many Bolivian women wear traditional clothing like bowler hats, colourful shawls, and pollera skirts.
Political graffiti with MAS and Evo and objects painted black, white, and blue are clues for Bolivia.
Bolivia’s Wiphala flag, a colorful square patchwork, is its second official flag and often seen on government buildings.
Tigo telecom ads with a blue logo appear in urban Bolivia and help distinguish it from Peru.
Bolivia’s rocks and soil often have a distinct reddish tint, especially compared to nearby countries.
Coverage in Bolivia is limited mostly to six main cities, with side-street depth there, and main roads elsewhere.
The Altiplano is Bolivia’s vast highland grassland plateau, mostly flat with surrounding hills and mountains.
Northern Altiplano grasslands look more lush and green, especially near El Alto and La Paz.
Southern Altiplano is more arid, especially near Oruro and southwest towards Chile.
Lake Titicaca is Bolivia’s most important lake, visible from two main roads; landscape is greener than elsewhere in the west.
If surrounded by tall mountains, you are likely in Bolivia’s Andes region, which runs northwest to southeast.
East of the Andes is green, tropical, and flat, especially around Santa Cruz, with some large hills and pink soil.
Unpaved roads with pink soil occur around Santa Cruz in Bolivia’s tropical east.
La Paz and El Alto are twin cities but look different; see below for details.
La Paz is hilly, often located in valleys with green vegetation on the slopes.
Downtown La Paz is the only area in Bolivia with very tall buildings (10+ storeys).
Many parts of La Paz have pillar-like rock formations of yellow-beige sandstone, unique among Bolivian cities.
El Alto sits on a flat, dusty plateau with a grid layout. Red brick semi-finished buildings dominate.
El Alto uses grey bricks with wavy edges for pavement, which is very common there.
El Alto’s Neo-Andean architecture features colorful, futuristic facades; almost unique to this city.
In El Alto, doors and gates are sometimes painted with gradient patterns.
Cochabamba lies in a flat valley with a wall of mountains to the north, a unique city identifier.
Oruro is in a very dry, flat landscape with a dry hill usually visible to the west.
Sucre is very hilly with many elevation changes; round, tree-covered hills are common.
Sucre's historic city center has colonial buildings with white walls and orange tiled roofs.
Potosí is hilly and arid, with little or no trees on the hills.
The Cerro Rico mountain dominates Potosí, its surface stripped bare by mining for silver.
Santa Cruz is Bolivia’s only major city in a tropical, flat landscape.
Ruta 1 west of El Alto runs through green grasslands and near Lake Titicaca; white-numbered markings often seen.
Ruta 3 near Pongo is famous for enormous mountains with low-hanging clouds and dark grey rock.
The N Yungas Road ('Death Road') is a bendy, unpaved, tropical mountain road, dangerously foggy in parts.
Bolivia’s only large divided highway is Ruta 1/4 between La Paz and Oruro through the Altiplano.
A long section of Ruta 4 has a distinct square camera smudge from Vila Vila through Cochabamba to Buena Vista.
The Morochata area, NW of Cochabamba on Ruta 25, has mountain dirt roads and eucalyptus, looking much like Peru.
Ruta 1 near Challapata is arid, with patches of snow; weather ranges from cloudy to overcast.
North of Challapata: straight flat roads with hills, improved weather and blue sky when looking south.
South of Challapata: curvy and hilly roads with notably grey skies.
A section of Ruta 7 near Santa Cruz has a visual glitch from a camera bug, seen as neon discoloration.
The Mataral area has very green, hilly landscapes and sunny weather with low but abundant vegetation.
Here, you’ll often spot large cacti and trees with yellow flowers among the bushes.
Eastern Ruta 4 is flat and green, with asphalt and concrete sections and occasional low hills.
Around Chaco, Ruta 5 features sunset coverage, concrete pavement and winds through semi-arid hills.
Southwest of Patacamaya, Ruta 4 has worn-down grainy asphalt through semi-arid grasslands.
Southwest Ruta 4 offers views of Nevado Sajama, a unique snow-capped volcano only visible south of Callapa and in national park coverage.
Ruta 6 between Tarabuco and Zudáñez has extremely white concrete, unique to this road.
The road near Coipasa and Villa Catalina crosses arid desert terrain and a salt flat, with cone-shaped volcanoes visible.
Coverage of Sajama National Park features a unique Google car and open views of Nevado Sajama and adobe village buildings.
